summary: Trickle is a simple algorithm that lets nodes in lossy, low-power networks share information efficiently. Nodes adjust how often they transmit: they spread news quickly when things change, and stay mostly quiet when everyone is consistent. It is a building block used by other protocols for low-power networks.

eli5.summary: Neighbors in a village pass along news. If everyone already knows, they stay quiet and save energy. If something is new, they talk a lot until it has spread.

subtitle: A timer algorithm that makes nodes talk fast when data disagrees and almost not at all when it agrees.

tldr.problem: Nodes on a lossy shared medium, such as low-power wireless networks, need to keep data consistent without flooding the channel or wasting energy.
tldr.mechanism: A Trickle timer runs in intervals that double up to a maximum. A node transmits at a random point in the interval only if it has heard fewer than k consistent transmissions, and any inconsistency resets the interval to its minimum.
tldr.outcome: Nodes spread news within link-layer transmission times yet send only a few messages per hour when nothing changes. Protocols that use Trickle must define what counts as consistent.

today: RFC 6206 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself says Trickle has been used in a variety of protocols, in operational as well as academic settings.

sections.title: What Trickle Is For
sections.content:
The Trickle algorithm is a density-aware local communication primitive built on a consistency model that decides when a node transmits. When a node's data disagrees with its neighbors, it communicates quickly to resolve the inconsistency, for example in milliseconds. When nodes agree, they slow down exponentially, so each sends only a few packets per hour. Rather than flooding a network, each node hears a small trickle of packets, just enough to stay consistent.

Trickle relies only on local communication, such as broadcast or local multicast. It needs very little state: the RFC says current implementations use 4-11 bytes of RAM and 50-200 lines of C code. It was originally designed for reprogramming protocols, where the data is the program code, and has since been applied to control traffic timing, multicast propagation and route discovery.

The RFC describes the algorithm and gives guidelines. It does not present performance results or explain the design in detail.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the neighborhood shares news. When nothing is new, they whisper only once in a while. When something changes, they talk right away until everyone knows.

sections.title: The Basic Idea
sections.content:
Trickle's basic primitive: every so often, a node transmits data unless it hears a few other transmissions that make its own redundant. The data might be routing state, software update versions or the last multicast packet heard. Messages go to a local address: in IPv6 it can be the link-local multicast address or another local multicast address, and in IPv4 it can be the broadcast address.

There are two outcomes for a message. Either every receiver finds the data consistent with its own state, or some receiver finds an inconsistency. That can happen because an out-of-date node hears something new, or an updated node hears something old. If node A says it has version V and node B has version V+1, B learns that A needs an update, and if B speaks first, A learns the same. It does not matter who transmits first.

Because Trickle communication is either sending or hearing, it works in sparse and dense networks alike. In a lossless single-hop network of size n, each node's transmission rate is 1/n of the communication rate, so the load is balanced. Sparser networks need more transmissions per node, but the use of the shared channel does not rise, which matters in wireless networks.
sections.eli5: If you hear a friend say what you were about to say, you keep quiet. If your friend has old news, you correct them, and if you have old news, you learn it.

sections.title: Parameters and Variables
sections.content:
A Trickle timer has three configuration parameters:

  • Imin, the minimum interval size, in units of time such as milliseconds.
  • Imax, the maximum interval size, given as a number of doublings of Imin. For example, with Imin of 100 ms and Imax of 16, the longest interval is 100 ms * 65,536, or 6,553.6 seconds, about 109 minutes.
  • k, the redundancy constant, a natural number (an integer greater than zero).

It also keeps three variables: I, the current interval size; t, a time within the current interval; and c, a counter.
sections.eli5: There are three knobs: the shortest wait, how many times the wait may double, and how many repeats of the same news are enough to stay quiet.

sections.title: The Six Rules
sections.content:
The algorithm has six rules:

  1. On start, set I to a value between Imin and Imax, then begin the first interval.
  2. When an interval begins, reset c to 0 and set t to a random point in the range [I/2, I). The interval ends at I.
  3. Whenever a "consistent" transmission is heard, increment c.
  4. At time t, transmit if and only if c is less than k.
  5. When the interval expires, double I. If that exceeds the time specified by Imax, set I to the Imax time.
  6. On hearing an "inconsistent" transmission, if I is greater than Imin, reset the timer by setting I to Imin and starting a new interval as in rule 2. If I already equals Imin, do nothing. External "events" may also reset the timer.

The words consistent, inconsistent and events are quoted because their meaning depends on the protocol using Trickle. The only time Trickle transmits is rule 4, so there is deliberately a delay between detecting an inconsistency and responding. Responding immediately could cause a broadcast storm, with many nodes answering at once in sync. Following the algorithm with the minimal interval lets the protocol benefit from suppression across a huge range of node densities.
sections.eli5: Each round, you pick a random moment to speak, but only if you have not already heard enough friends say the same thing. Each quiet round lasts twice as long, until something surprising happens and you start over with short rounds.

sections.title: What a Protocol Using Trickle Must Specify
sections.content:
A protocol specification that uses Trickle MUST specify:

  • Default values for Imin, Imax and k. Because link layers vary, the default Imin SHOULD be given in terms of worst-case link-layer latency, for example "4 times the worst-case link-layer latency", not "500 milliseconds".
  • What counts as a "consistent" transmission.
  • What counts as an "inconsistent" transmission.
  • Which "events", besides inconsistent transmissions, reset the timer.
  • What information a node sends in Trickle messages.
  • What actions outside the algorithm, if any, the protocol takes on detecting an inconsistency.
sections.eli5: Trickle is only the timing rule. Whoever uses it still has to say what the news is and what counts as a surprise.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC RECOMMENDS that protocols using Trickle include a way to tell nodes their parameters at runtime. When nodes differ, odd behavior can result:

  • Mismatched k: nodes with a higher k transmit more often. A node with k=2 among nodes with k=1 can end up sending in every interval, which can drain energy in a low-power network.
  • Mismatched Imin: faster nodes may briefly suppress slower ones, but this ends after the first slow interval, so it is usually not a significant concern.
  • Mismatched Imax: nodes with small Imax transmit faster and suppress those with larger Imax, which then never transmit. This causes long-term inequities in energy cost.
  • Mismatched definitions of consistency: Trickle may fail to reach a consistent state. Consistency definitions MUST be clearly stated in the protocol and SHOULD NOT be configured at runtime.

Setting k to infinity disables suppression and is NOT RECOMMENDED, since every node then sends in every interval and dense networks can congest. A high k such as 5 or 10 is preferable, and typical values are 1-5. Because k=0 has no useful meaning, protocols that need to turn suppression off are RECOMMENDED to reserve k=0 to mean infinity. A protocol SHOULD also set k and Imin so that Imin is at least two to three times as long as it takes to transmit k packets.

The authors urge designers not to tweak Trickle without a great deal of experimental evidence, noting that it is not optimal but is simple and needs little state.
sections.eli5: If friends use different rules about when to talk, some get tired out and some never get a turn, so everyone should agree on the rules.

sections.title: Examples of Trickle in Use
sections.content:
The RFC gives two example uses and says they are not exhaustive.

Reliable flooding or dissemination: nodes advertise the newest data they have, typically as a version number. Hearing a newer version or new data is an inconsistency. Hearing an older or equal version is consistent. On hearing an older version, a node sends an update instead of resetting its own timer, and nodes that receive it reset theirs, so the data spreads quickly.

Routing control traffic: nodes use Trickle to time beacons carrying routing state. An inconsistency is a topology change that could cause loops or significant stretch, such as a detected loop or a large change in a node's routing cost. The routing protocol can react quickly with a small Imin yet send few beacons when stable. The RFC names the IPv6 routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks (RPL), the Collection Tree Protocol and some commercial IPv6 routing layers as examples.
sections.eli5: One use is passing a new rule book around a village. Another is telling neighbors when the road map changed, and otherwise staying quiet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As an algorithm, Trickle has no specific security considerations of its own, but two concerns arise when a protocol uses it.

First, an adversary can force many extra packets by forcing timer resets, which can shorten the life of a low-power network. Protocols can limit this by carefully choosing what can cause a reset and protecting those events and messages, for example by authenticating a packet that resets nearby timers.

Second, an adversary can try to keep nodes from becoming consistent by suppressing transmissions with "consistent" messages. Authenticated messages or a transitive notion of consistency can help. The RFC argues that on a shared broadcast medium an adversary cannot both silence node A and avoid notifying A's neighbors, and notes that Trickle should filter unicast messages.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker could shout fake surprises to make everyone talk constantly, so important messages should be signed.
